description: NextGenLab olarak, yapay zekâ ve robotik kodlama eğitimleriyle öğrencilerimizin merakını keşfe, fikirlerini üretime dönüştürüyoruz. Çeşitli robotik yarışmalarında takım çalışması ve problem çözme becerilerini geliştiren öğrencilerimizle, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026’da yer almaktan heyecan duyuyoruz. Teknoloji üreten, birlikte öğrenen ve geleceğe yön veren bir nesil için çalışıyoruz. 🚀
summary:
TWENTY is an on-board health monitoring and decision-support app for deep-space crews. A message between Mars and Earth can take up to about 20 minutes one way, so in our scenario a sick astronaut waits 24 minutes for a doctor's answer. TWENTY makes the first decision on board, even without internet.

It reads a real pulse from an off-the-shelf smartwatch over Web Bluetooth, rules out dangerous causes step by step (oxygen, ECG, blood sugar, cabin CO2, other crew, symptoms) and explains its reasoning as likelihood, reasons and next steps, never as a diagnosis. In our night-palpitations scenario it reached "suspected heart rhythm problem" in 34 seconds. A VR scene for Meta Quest runs an eyes-closed balance test and a memory and reaction test, and lets a flight surgeon watch a live twin of the ship with the real communication delay. After a Mars landing, TWENTY answers "fit for duty?" in about 2 minutes.

Every feature maps to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, and a hazard chain shows how risks that look yellow alone become red together.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

TWENTY is the doctor for the 20 minutes when Earth cannot answer. On a Mars mission, a message to Earth can take up to about 20 minutes one way. If an astronaut gets sick at night, the flight surgeon's answer arrives far too late. TWENTY makes the first, safest decision on board and explains why.

HOW IT WORKS

- Health overview: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, temperature, blood sugar, sleep and mood, each against the astronaut's own range.

- Triage, "rule out danger first": for sudden palpitations, TWENTY checks oxygen, heart rate onset, ECG rhythm, blood sugar, cabin CO2, other crew and symptoms. It shows a likelihood (for example "suspected heart rhythm problem", SVT pattern), the reasons, and what to do now. It never diagnoses; the crew medical officer and flight surgeon decide.

- Mission mode with four playable scenarios: S1 Night 03:12 (palpitations: panic attack or rhythm problem?), S2 Hatch (head impact: red flags, reaction and memory tests, overnight wake-up check), S4 Solar storm (onboard dosimeter, shelter and dose tracking), S5 Mars landing (balance, standing heart rate and attention: fit for duty?).

- Hazard chain: NASA says the hazards "can feed off one another". TWENTY shows how sleep loss, cabin CO2 and a night in the radiation shelter look acceptable one by one but together lead to "no solo spacewalk today".

- Real sensor: a commercial smartwatch streams real heart rate to TWENTY over Web Bluetooth (standard Heart Rate Service). In the stand-up test we measured 75 to 81 bpm with a real watch.

- VR: a WebXR scene for Meta Quest. The astronaut takes an eyes-closed balance test (head sway) and a memory and reaction test inside the headset. An observer view lets a flight surgeon on "Earth" watch a live twin of the ship with an 11:53 delay.

- AI Doctor chat with an offline fallback, so the app still answers without a connection.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Faster, safer decisions: in our S1 test the time from alarm to a reasoned decision was 34 seconds instead of waiting about 24 minutes for Earth.

- Low cost: an off-the-shelf watch, a consumer VR headset and a web address. No custom hardware.

- On Earth: the same balance and stand-up tests could help screen fall risk in older adults and support care in remote places without a doctor (this mode is a concept today).

NASA ALIGNMENT

Every alert is tagged with one of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile closed environment). The communication delay is shown live on screen to make "distance from Earth" visible.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, Three.js with React Three Fiber and React Three XR (WebXR for Meta Quest), Web Bluetooth, Trystero (peer-to-peer live link between app, watch page and VR observer), Vercel hosting. Hardware: Huawei smartwatch, Meta Quest headset, laptop. Demo video made with Remotion. SI use: the demo narration voice is AI-generated with ElevenLabs (script written by our team), and code was written with help from Claude (Anthropic).

WHAT IS REAL AND WHAT IS SIMULATED

Scenario vital signs are simulated. The smartwatch heart rate and the VR test results are real measurements. Thresholds are representative and would need flight surgeon approval and personal preflight values. TWENTY is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It treats the communication delay as the core problem, explains every decision instead of giving a black-box score, and turns cheap consumer devices into a crew health station.
